The floor is yours. Good afternoon. Thank you for allowing us some time to give an update

on special programs admission data for the '26, '27 school year. This presentation will follow the here's what, so what, now what framework. We will first review what the admissions data tells us about student interest and enrollment, then discuss what the findings mean, including notable strengths and opportunities, and finally outline next steps for outreach and program adjustments. Our goal is to use data to inform decisions that support equitable access

and align program offerings with student and family interests. The full report is located in your folder and is also in Board Docs. I want to take a quick moment to thank our partners from the research office for putting together our data packet. We couldn't do this without their help and support. This includes detailed admissions, enrollment, and demographic data for all special programs. Today's presentation focuses on the major

trends related to student interest compared to enrollment across our secondary programs and the elementary dual language immersion program. It is important to note that this year the accepted tables reflect the number of students enrolled on September 30th. This is a change from past years in which we included students enrolled prior to the start of the school year. We wanted to present transparent data that better indicates the students

actually participating in these programs this year. This September 30th date also aligns with the VDOE reporting date. Here is our special programs life cycle. From August through January, our focus is on promoting on recruiting for all of our special programs, ensuring students and families are aware of the opportunities available to them. In November, today at this meeting, we share our admissions data

from the previous year. This review allows us to reflect on participation trends, identify areas of success, and consider adjustments that may strengthen future recruitment and enrollment efforts. In March, we will shift our focus to enrolling and preparing newly admitted students for successful program placement. In May, we move into the review and evaluation phase. Program owners will come to SPC meeting and present an overview of their program,

including retention data, key accomplishments, highlights, and opportunities for improvement. During the summer months is when we use that feedback and data from the year to refine our programs and prepare for the next admission cycle, which begins again with the start of that new school year. Several of our newer programs are still in the implementation phase and are adding grade levels each year.

Access is in its second year, AGLS is in its first year. HAMSCI is continuing its phased expansion, and dual language immersion is still growing into the upper elementary grades. Because these programs are relatively new, we expect participation patterns to continue evolving as awareness grows and programs become fully established. At this time, several established programs, including AET, AOS, MATA, IB at Heritage and Long Valley, and

NJROTC, now provide multiple years of trend data that help us better understand long-term student interest. It is important to recognize that our programs utilize different admissions models. AET, Advanced AET, and AOS use a competitive, merit-based process. Our MATA and NJROTC use prerequisite-based qualification with lottery selection, while Access,

AGLS, HAMSCI, IB, and dual language immersion use lottery-based admissions. These differing admissions structures influence enrollment rates and should be considered when comparing program data. This slide illustrates the gap between student interest and actual enrollment across our secondary special programs. While application numbers are strong across nearly all programs, available seats naturally limit enrollment.

Programs such as MATA, AET, and AOS continue to attract substantial interest, while newer options such as Access, AGLS, and HAMSCI are also demonstrating strong demand. The chart highlights both the popularity of these opportunities and the ongoing importance of aligning capacity with student interest when possible. It is important to note that everyone interested in both AGLS and IB were offered a seat and no wait list remained this year.

Next, the dual language immersion program continues to generate strong family interest, though demand varies by location. This year, Potomac transitioned from a regional enrollment model to a school priority model. Sanders Corner remains the regional program with 50% of seats reserved for students within the attendance zone and 50% of students from outside the zone. It is also important to note that we offered all available seats in our DLI

program at Leesburg at this time. Moving on to our so what. After reviewing the admissions data, the next step is understanding what the data tells us about student interest, access, and participation. We focused on three questions: What trends stand out in the data? Where are we seeing success? And where are the opportunities to strengthen awareness or participation among specific communities?

Across the secondary special programs, students submitted 9,170 applications, while 1,587 students ultimately enrolled, resulting in an overall enrollment rate of 17.3%. MATA generated the highest number of applications with 2,845 applicants, followed by AET with 1,756 applicants. ACCESS and AET were among the most competitive programs, with enrollment

rates of approximately 6.4% and 8.2% respectively. These numbers demonstrate substantial student interest in specialized academic and career-focused experiences throughout the division. One clear strength is the breadth of special program opportunities available to students. A huge thank you to this committee and the entire school board for making these opportunities possible for our students here in LCPS.

MATA applications increased by 46% compared to 2022, reflecting sustained interest in career and technical education pathways. And I just want to acknowledge that we have Dr. Grubbs here, and he is a huge part of our success with our career and technical education. Our HAMCI applications increased by 26% in just one year. ACCESS applications more than doubled from 211 to 440

applications, while NJROTC applications also increased dramatically even after accounting for the change this year that requires in-zone Loudoun County High School students to also apply for the program. Although AET and AOS applications have declined slightly over several years, they continue to attract more than 1,500 applicants each and remain highly sought-after programs. These trends indicate strong interest across a diverse profile of program offerings.

The data also reveals opportunities to broaden participation across the division. Interest in many programs is concentrated within specific geographic areas. For example, four middle schools account for nearly half of all AET and AOS applications. Similar patterns appear across several lottery programs, where a relatively small number of school communities generate a large percentage of applications. These trends suggest opportunities to continue

expanding awareness and outreach in communities that may be less familiar with available special program options. Now on to the now what. Based on these findings, our next steps focus on two primary areas. First, we strengthen outreach and awareness efforts to ensure families understand the opportunities available to them. Second, we will continue refining program structures and admission process

to better align with demonstrated student interest while maintaining accessibility and transparency. Creating awareness remains one of our most important strategies in our outreach efforts. We want every student and family to have access to clear, timely information about program opportunities so they can make informed decisions based on their interests and goals. Our outreach efforts are designed to reach students through multiple channels and at multiple points throughout the admissions cycle.

Our outreach strategies include special program fairs. We hold two of them. We had one at Heritage High School and one at Park View High School this year. We also have a panel at that event where we have students from all programs represented so that our families and students can actually talk to students that are currently in the programs. Each program does hold its own information night throughout the fall. We do middle school visits. We do an assembly at every school.

We have our websites for each program. We have videos. We have admission timelines that we have gotten on track together so that offers and everything go out at the same time. We also have our annual special programs magazine that is located in your folder as well. Together, these resources provide families with multiple opportunities to learn about programs, ask questions, and understand application requirements. We will continue evaluating these efforts to ensure

information is accessible and reaches students across all of our school communities. The next one you've heard a lot about. We've had many conversations about this, but we are really excited that we are expanding awareness of all our special programs through our Future Ready Exploration Lesson. This is scheduled for next Thursday, November 12th. It's a district-wide exploration lesson at all middle schools.

By embedding this common exploration activity, we can ensure all students across LCPS are exposed to available opportunities, regardless of whether they actively seek out program information on their own. A review of application data shows that many students applied to multiple programs, which can inflate overall interest figures and make it difficult to accurately gauge program demand. Allowing students to apply to unlimited programs also introduces

logistical challenges with managing and working through waitlists as students accept some opportunities and decline others. As we've stated before, beginning this year, students may indicate interest in up to two lottery programs while still maintaining the ability to apply to AET, AOS, and TJ. This adjustment is intended to provide more meaningful measures of student interest, while still preserving opportunities for students to explore multiple

pathways. As such, future versions of this data may show decreased interest. However, this decline would be superficial only and would result from requiring students and families to be more focused in their program application decisions. We've also updated the admissions process by moving parent or guardian approval to the beginning of the application. An application is only considered complete when both the student

submits and parent approves, and those need to be received by the deadline in order to be included in the lotteries. This change helps ensure that applicants have family support before entering the admissions process and provides a more accurate picture of actual interest and intent to enroll in that program. This concludes the admissions data review. We welcome feedback and discussion regarding the trends presented tonight,

as well as suggestions related to outreach, recruitment, and future program development. Our goal is to continue ensuring that special programs reflect student interests and provide meaningful opportunities for learners across Loudoun County Public Schools. Thank you so much. trends. I know personally, I am really curious to see where we are in a year after narrowing the scope of how many programs kids can apply to. is going to really broaden the scope for kids, as it is really going to drive home the availability of the programs, and I hope to see that more spread out across the county as that rolls out. accelerate into these academic programs, specialized programs, I'm often worried that groups will get left behind. what do we do about that? I think one of the things that I'm concerned about is, is it a self-efficacy thing?
